account: University of Michigan researchers worked with Flint’s service-line replacement program from summer 2016. ActiveRemediation used property records and confirmed pipe materials to recommend inspections. Its held-out prediction accuracy was 91.6%. The researchers reported that the program had replaced hazardous lines at 4,419 homes by September 2017. They wrote that their modeling had less influence on the choice of replacement homes, because those choices faced political and logistical limits. In a separate simulation they estimated that their method would have lowered the cost per successful replacement from the observed US$5,818 to about US$5,196. That is a saving of about US$622 per replacement, or 10.7%. Independent reporting later documented a decline in inspection success after the contractor changed its approach, alongside changes in geography and policy. A March 2019 court order required prioritization using the model’s address lists. Wired reported in January 2021 that Flint had resumed using the model and that nearly 10,000 lead pipes had been replaced by the end of 2020. In March 2023 Pierre Goovaerts of BioMedware, who has no tie to the developers, compared the program's excavation order from 2016 to 2020 with geostatistical rankings. He found that the program's order found lead lines fastest in its first eight months and that the rankings would have done better after that. He concluded that the 2018 decision to stop using the model does not explain this weaker relative result. In July 2025 the Natural Resources Defense Council said that nearly 11,000 pipes had been replaced as the state reported completion to the court. The field evidence does not isolate the model’s effect on residents’ health or on realized spending.

display.answer: Crews inspected pipes and recorded their materials. Researchers used those results to update predictions and recommend further inspections.

value.text: Crews inspected pipes and recorded their materials. Researchers used those results to update predictions and recommend further inspections.

purpose: The model and active-learning rules were built to predict which Flint homes had lead or galvanized service lines and to direct inspections and replacements. The improved hit rate was the intended use.

ratings.reason: Residents benefited from identification and replacement of hazardous service lines, without a measured health effect attributable to the model.
The program gained a measured capability to predict pipe materials and prioritize work.

Flint replaced hazardous service lines at 4,419 homes by September 2017. In July 2025 the Natural Resources Defense Council said that nearly 11,000 pipes had been replaced. The model helped prioritize inspections for part of that period.

must_hold: Official use of the predictions alongside local needs

summary: ActiveRemediation, a model built at the University of Michigan, ranked Flint homes for inspection and replacement of lead or galvanized-steel service lines, with 91.6% held-out accuracy.
system: ActiveRemediation, combining XGBoost predictions, a hierarchical Bayesian spatial model, and active learning
